en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-vinayaviniścaya-sūtra*:
All catalogues state that this was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from Dunhuang.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

At the Solitary Hermitage, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus and ten thousand bodhisattvas, the World-Honored One then gazed upon the great assembly as a dragon king surveys its domain. Having observed the assembly, he addressed the bodhisattvas:
"O virtuous ones!"
"Who will be able, in the future evil age, to endure and uphold the True Dharma, and by means of various skillful expedients bring sentient beings to fulfillment?
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

I am able to endure, for the sake of future generations, upholding the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* accumulated by the Tathāgata over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta-asamkhyeya* kalpas, thereby bringing great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Siṃha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to endure and bring sentient beings to maturity.”
The Bodhisattva Vajra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to endure, out of compassion, to protect and guard all wicked sentient beings.”
The Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to endure and fulfill all the hopes and aspirations of sentient beings.”
The Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to endure and bring about the removal of ignorance for all sentient beings.”
The Bodhisattva Dharmavijaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to endure and bring all sentient beings to leave behind all that is contrary to the Dharma.”
The Bodhisattva Candravijaya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to endure and bring it about that all sentient beings may always remain far removed from dharmas that are not meritorious.”
The Bodhisattva Daysheng addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to endure using the vehicle of peace and happiness to enable all sentient beings to attain liberation.”
The Bodhisattva Abhayamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to endure and accomplish the benefit and welfare of boundless sentient beings.”
The Bodhisattva Gadaprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to endure and expound the Dharma of non-delusion, so that all sentient beings may hear and know it, thereby accomplishing wisdom.”
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to endure and give rise to great vows, so that all inexhaustible sentient beings may achieve fulfillment.”
The Bodhisattva Candraprabha said,
“I am able to endure bringing about the constant performance of service for all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Sunetra said:
“I am able to endure providing the root of peace and happiness for all sentient beings.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said:
“I am able to endure acting as a refuge for those sentient beings who are stubborn and in the evil realms.”
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said:
“I am able to endure [the task] of bringing across all sentient beings who have not yet been delivered from the evil realms.
The Bodhisattva Susaṃkhyeya said:
"I am able to endure bringing those sentient beings who are unsubdued into subjection.
The Bodhisattva Wonderful Intention (or Wonderful Sound) said:
"I am able to endure bringing those sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings to liberation."
The Bodhisattva Joyful Delight said,
“I am able to endure and bring to fulfillment even those beings who are lowly, base, evil, and defiled.
The Bodhisattva Accumulated Light said:
"I am able to endure bringing to fulfillment those sentient beings who are animals and lead them to liberation.
The Bodhisattva Entry into Non-contention said:
"I am able to endure manifesting the right path to bring sentient beings to fulfillment."
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said,
“I am able to endure providing peace, happiness, and benefit to sentient beings in order to seek true wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Acintya said:
"I am able to endure and compassionately bring to fulfillment those beings who are hungry ghosts.
The Bodhisattva Sunlight said,
"I am able to endure and bring to maturity those beings who have not yet reached full maturity."
The Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha said:
"I am able to endure and fulfill all the wishes of sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Mahābalin said:
"I am able to endure closing the gates of the evil realms for the sake of all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Severing Doubt said,
"I am able to endure bringing those sentient beings who delight in inferior dharmas to liberation."
The Bodhisattva Abiding in Fearlessness said:
"I am able to endure constantly benefiting sentient beings through praise.
The Bodhisattva Auspicious Victorious Wisdom said:
"I am able to endure following the various inclinations of all sentient beings to deliver and liberate them," said the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Immeasurable.
"I am able to endure preaching the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) for all sentient beings."
The Bodhisattva Abiding in Fearlessness Toward All Dharmas said:
"I am able to endure and bring joy to those sentient beings who delight in various vehicles, manifesting them according to their respective inclinations."
The Bodhisattva Subhāṣita said,
“I am able to endure constantly showing sentient beings those things they delight in, so as to bring them to fulfillment.
The Bodhisattva Vimalajvālā said:
“I am able to endure loving-kindness toward sentient beings, protecting them so that they may achieve fulfillment.
Bodhisattva Maṇiprabha said:
“I am able to endure bringing about the realization of past lives for all sentient beings.”
The Bodhisattva Prabhāśrī said,
“I am able to endure and, through right effort, rescue sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Bhadraśrī said:
"I am able to endure [the task] of ultimately severing the suffering and affliction of sentient beings.
Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi said:
"I am able to endure [the task] of bestowing various precious jewels upon sentient beings to bring them peace and happiness."
The Bodhisattva Supreme Intent said,
"I am able to endure [the task of] causing impoverished sentient beings to be free from the suffering of poverty.
The Bodhisattva Severing All Bonds said:
“I am able to endure ensuring that all sentient beings always remain far removed from the terrors of affliction.
Bodhisattva Vajraprabha said,
“I am able to endure manifesting the true path for all sentient beings.”
The Bodhisattva Manifesting Virtuous Form said, "I am able to endure those beings who seek much; I can provide for them all according to their requests.
The Bodhisattva Dharma-udaya said:
"I am able to endure constantly teaching the practice of all pure dharmas.
The Bodhisattva Vajrakāya said:
"I am able to endure removing all obstacles for all sentient beings."
The Bodhisattva Dharmahita said:
"I am able to endure and constantly deliver sentient beings by means of the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Alpaśruta (in the Dan translation: *Alpa*) said:
"I am able to endure acting for the sake of all sentient beings by eliminating their various poisons.
The Bodhisattva Candrottara said:
"I am able to endure acting for the sake of all sentient beings by manifesting and preaching the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Siṃhamati said:
"I am able to endure constantly benefiting sentient beings through the gift of the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Kumāraprabha said:
"I am able to endure delivering all sentient beings who dwell in lowly states," said the Bodhisattva Buddhaguṇa.
"I am able to endure manifesting the Right Path to sever all evil destinies."
The Bodhisattva Vajraprabha said,
“I am able to endure manifesting physical forms and images to deliver sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Śrīvijaya said:
“I am able to endure bringing about the welfare of sentient beings who are otherwise being diminished.
Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvara said:
“I am able to endure closing the gates of hell.”
The Bodhisattva Amṛtadhara said,
"I am able to endure bringing all sentient beings across birth and death.
The Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha said:
“I am able to endure, for the sake of all sentient beings, constantly manifesting radiance to extinguish all fetters.

At that time, Śāriputra, hearing how these bodhisattvas thus accomplished sentient beings as their own adornment, attained what he had never experienced before and came forward to address the Buddha, saying:
“It is unprecedented! It is marvelous!”
“World-Honored One!

These bodhisattvas possess inconceivable great compassion; they adorn themselves with various skillful means and firm diligence, such that no sentient beings can obstruct, measure, equal, or subdue them, and their radiance cannot be obscured.”
“World-Honored One!

I constantly praise these bodhisattvas for their unprecedented deeds: namely, that when someone comes to them and requests their head, eyes, ears, nose, body, hands, feet, or any other possession, at the time of such a request they feel no stinginess and do not give rise to a mind of regret.”

"Bhagavān! I constantly reflect and always think this: if there are those who oppress these bodhisattvas, seeking from them all things, whether internal or external, you should know that they are all bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation."
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

These matters concerning the spheres of meditative concentration, skillful means, and wisdom possessed by these bodhisattvas are beyond the capacity for deliberation of all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

although these bodhisattvas witness the supernatural transformations and miraculous powers of the Buddhas, their minds do not waver regarding all phenomena, and they constantly fulfill the various desires and aspirations of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If there are sentient beings who delight in the way of householders, he manifests in the form of a householder for the sake of their accomplishment.
If there are sentient beings who delight in great majesty and power, he manifests as various kings possessing great sovereign might to subdue them."
If there are sentient beings who aspire to seek nirvana, he delivers them by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
For those who seek the state of a Pratyekabuddha, he manifests in the form of a Pratyekabuddha for the sake of delivering them.
Those who seek the Mahāyāna path manifest in the body of a Buddha in order to establish all the Buddha-dharmas.
"In this way, Śāriputra, these bodhisattvas,
through various skillful means, bring sentient beings to maturity, causing them all to abide securely in the Buddha-dharma."

Why is this so? Śāriputra, if one were to exclude the wisdom of the Tathāgata, there would be no other vehicle by which one could attain liberation and reach nirvāṇa; for this reason, he is called the Tathāgata.
Why is this so? It is because when the Tathāgata speaks of the dharma of suchness, he awakens to this dharma as it truly is; thus he is called the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, knowing the various inclinations and desires of all sentient beings and manifesting himself accordingly, he is called the Tathāgata.
One who has accomplished all roots of goodness and severed all roots of unwholesomeness is called a Tathāgata;
one who can show sentient beings the path to liberation is called a Tathāgata;
one who can cause sentient beings to distance themselves from false paths and manifest the noble path is called a Tathāgata.
One who expounds all dharmas of emptiness to manifest the meaning of emptiness is called a Tathāgata;

one who, according to the various consciousnesses and diverse inclinations of all sentient beings, reveals the path to liberation in accordance with their respective preferences is called a Tathāgata.

The delusive thoughts and doubts of ordinary beings can cause them to perceive what is not the true Dharma; however, the Bodhisattvas do not give rise to movement or fluctuation within the various dharma-realms, and they bring all illusory sentient beings to liberation, gradually proceeding toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a lay bodhisattva should practice two kinds of giving. What are these two?
The first is the gift of material wealth;
the second is the gift of the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
A renunciant bodhisattva, gentle and free from anger, should practice the four kinds of giving.
What are these four? First, paper;
Second, ink; third, a brush; fourth, the Dharma.
These four kinds of giving are what those who have left the household life should practice.
Bodhisattvas who have attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) should cultivate three kinds of giving.
What are these three?

They are the giving away of one’s royal throne, the giving away of one’s wife and children, and the giving away of one’s head, eyes, and limbs. These three types of giving are called "great giving" and "supremely wondrous giving. Bodhisattvas who have attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) should practice these three kinds of giving.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
should a bodhisattva not fear desire, hatred, and delusion?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“There are two major transgressions for a bodhisattva. What are these two?”
Violating the precepts due to hatred and delusion is called a "great offense," whereas violating them due to desire is called a "small offense" that is difficult to eliminate.
Violating the precepts due to hatred is called a "great offense" that is easy to eliminate;
violating them due to delusion is also called a "great offense," yet it is likewise difficult to eliminate.
For what reason is craving considered a minor transgression yet difficult to eliminate?
Craving can increase the branches of birth and death and also serves as their seed; for this reason, though it is small, it is difficult to dispel.
Those who commit offenses out of anger fall into the hells, the animal realm, and the evil destinies; these can quickly create obstacles for the mind, yet they are easy to eliminate.
Those who commit offenses out of delusion fall into the eight great hells and various places of great suffering, from which it is difficult to attain liberation.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If there is a bodhisattva who violates the first precept, they should repent with an upright mind and profound sincerity before ten members of the assembly; one who has intentionally violated a precept should repent with an upright mind and profound sincerity before five members of the assembly;
or, if one has grasped a woman’s hand or looked upon her with an evil mind, one should repent with an upright mind and profound sincerity before either one person or two people."

"If there is a bodhisattva who commits one of the five *ānantarya* sins—whether by violating a woman or a man, or through intentional transgression, or by offending a stūpa, or by offending the Saṃgha—and other such remaining offenses, that bodhisattva should, in the presence of the thirty-five Buddhas, alone in a secluded place day and night, with a sincere mind, repent for the grave sins committed."
The method of repentance is as follows:
take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha.
"Namo Śākyamuni Buddha; Namo Vajrābhedyabuddha; Namo Ratna..."
Homage to the Buddha Prabhāsa; Homage to the Buddha Nāgeśvararāja; Homage to the Buddha Vīryasena;
Homage to the Buddha Vīryaprabha; Homage to the Buddha Ratnāgni; Homage to the Buddha Ratnacandraprabha;
Homage to the Buddha Abhīmukha; Homage to the Buddha Ratnacandra; Homage to the Buddha Vimala; Homage to the Buddha Vigatamala.
Buddha; Homage to the Buddha Vīradatta; Homage to the Buddha Viśuddha; Homage to the Buddha Viśuddhadatta;
Homage to the Buddha Varuṇa; Homage to the Buddha Varuṇadeva; Homage to the Buddha Dṛḍhaśrī; Homage to the Buddha Candanaśrī; Homage to the Buddha Amitoṣṇaraśmi; Homage to the Buddha Prabhāśrī.
Buddha! Homage to the Buddha Aśoka-guṇa; homage to the Buddha Nārāyaṇa; homage to the Buddha Guṇakusuma;
homage to the Buddha Padmaprabha-vikrīḍita-ṛddhi; homage to the Buddha Dhana-guṇa;
homage to the Buddha Guṇanidhyāna; homage to the Tathāgata Sukhābhidhāna-guṇa; homage to the Red...
Homage to the Tathāgata Jvālaketurāja; Homage to the Tathāgata Sugatigamanaguṇa;
Homage to the Tathāgata Saṃgrāmavijayin; Homage to the Tathāgata Sugati; Homage to the Tathāgata Samantavyūhaguṇa;
Homage to the Tathāgata Ratnakusumagati; Homage to the Tathāgata Ratnapadmasupratiṣṭhitaśāla...
"O Tathāgata King of Aśoka Trees!

In all such worlds as these, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, eternally abide in the world. I pray that all the World-Honored Ones will look upon me with compassion and pity. Whether in this life or in previous lives, from the beginningless cycle of birth and death until now, whatever various sins I have committed—whether committed by myself, caused others to commit, or rejoiced in seeing others commit them—"
Whether it be a stūpa, the Saṃgha, or the property of the Saṃgha from the four quarters—whether one takes it oneself, instructs another to take it, or sees it being taken and rejoices in it;
or regarding the five ānantarya crimes—whether one commits them oneself, instructs another to commit them, or sees them being committed and rejoices in them.
Regarding the ten unwholesome paths of action— whether committed by oneself, incited in others, or rejoiced in upon seeing them performed—

and whatever karmic obstructions have been created, whether concealed or unconcealed, which ought to lead to rebirth in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, the animal realm, or other evil destinies, such as the borderlands, low castes, and the Mlecchas— I now repent for all such karmic obstructions.
“May all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bear witness to me and keep me in mind.
Furthermore, before all the World-Honored Ones, one should speak these words:

“Whatever giving I have practiced in this life or in other lives, or whatever pure precepts I have observed; even if it were but a single mouthful of food given to an animal; or whatever roots of goodness from practicing pure conduct, whatever roots of goodness from bringing sentient beings to maturity, whatever roots of goodness from cultivating bodhi, and whatever roots of goodness from supreme wisdom—all these, collected together, calculated, and weighed, I dedicate entirely toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Just as the Buddhas of the past, future, and present have performed dedication, so too do I dedicate.”
I repent of all transgressions, rejoice in all merits,
and through the merit of inviting the Buddhas, may I attain supreme wisdom.
The Buddhas of the past, future, and present are the most supreme among all sentient beings.
"To the ocean of immeasurable merit, I take refuge and pay homage with palms joined.

"In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva contemplates these thirty-five Buddhas as if they were before their eyes and reflects upon all the merits of the Tathāgatas, they should perform such a pure confession."

Once a bodhisattva has been able to purify these offenses, at that time all Buddhas will manifest their bodies before them; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they also teach various practices in order to bring to maturity those beings who are ignorant and deluded.

The Bodhisattva’s mind remains unshakable within the realm of all phenomena (dharmadhātu), yet for all sentient beings who possess various desires and inclinations, he is able to deliver them according to their respective wishes and fulfill their aspirations.
If a bodhisattva enters the samādhi of great compassion, they can manifest entry into the hells, the animal realm, and all other evil destinies;
if a bodhisattva enters the samādhi of great adornment, they manifest the body of a layperson to bring sentient beings to maturity;
if a bodhisattva enters the samādhi of wondrous supremacy, they can manifest the body of a universal monarch (cakravartin) to bring sentient beings to maturity.
If a bodhisattva enters the *prabhāsa* samādhi, they can manifest the sublime physical forms of Śakra and Brahmā to bring sentient beings to maturity;
if a bodhisattva enters the *ekacitta* samādhi, they manifest the forms of śrāvakas to bring sentient beings to maturity;
if a bodhisattva enters the *viśuddha-advaya* samādhi, they manifest the forms of pratyekabuddhas to bring sentient beings to maturity.
If a bodhisattva enters the samādhi of tranquility, they can manifest the body of a Buddha to bring sentient beings to maturity;
if a bodhisattva enters the samādhi of mastery over all phenomena, they manifest various forms according to the diverse desires and inclinations of sentient beings to bring them to maturity.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva may manifest the body of Śakra, or manifest the body of Brahmā, or at times manifest the body of a wheel-turning monarch; all these are for the sake of bringing sentient beings to fulfillment, yet this bodhisattva does not waver from the realm of all phenomena (dharmadhātu).

Why is this? Although they manifest various forms in accordance with the diverse desires and inclinations of sentient beings, these bodhisattvas do not perceive a self or sentient beings, yet they manifest various bodies in accordance with those beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when the lion,
king of beasts, lets out a great roar, are the other small insects able to endure it? "No, they are not."
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, as for the heavy burden carried by a fragrant elephant, could donkeys, mules, and the like endure it? “No, they could not.”
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, could a poor person endure the majestic power, radiance, and physical form possessed by Śakra and Brahmā?
“No, World-Honored One.”
“World-Honored One!
“Furthermore, Śāriputra, what do you think?”
"Could birds such as vultures or pigeons endure the power possessed by the king of the garuḍas? "No,
World-Honored One."

"So it is, Śāriputra! By the power of the roots of goodness and the courageous resolve of a bodhisattva, and by relying on the wisdom of renunciation regarding all their transgressions, they attain visions of the Buddhas and achieve samādhi; this cannot be achieved by any sentient beings, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas through the mere removal of the remorse for their committed offenses."

If a bodhisattva can recite the names of all those Buddhas and constantly practice three things throughout the day and night, they will be free from committing offenses and from all sorrow and regret, and will further attain samādhi.
At that time, Upāli arose from meditative concentration and went to where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
While sitting alone in a quiet place, reflecting in meditation, he gave rise to this thought:

"The Tathāgata has taught these precepts of the pure *pratimokṣa*, which should be well-studied for the sake of those in the vehicles of the *śrāvaka*, *pratyekabuddha*, and *bodhisattva*; thus he spoke these words: 'One would rather sacrifice one's body and life than abandon the precepts.'"
"World-Honored One!
Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, what is called the prātimokṣa for those of the Śrāvaka vehicle?
And what is called the prātimokṣa for those of the Bodhisattva vehicle?"
The World-Honored One has declared that I am foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya; how then shall I extensively expound it for others?
Now, having heard it directly from the World-Honored One and received it with full retention, I have attained fearlessness, and only then can I extensively expound it for others.
While sitting alone in a secluded place, I reflected and had this thought:
"I should now go to the presence of the World-Honored One and inquire about the definitive meaning within the Vinaya."
"Now this great assembly of bodhisattvas and the community of bhikṣus have all gathered together.
Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"I only pray that you will explain this.
At that time, the World-Honored One told Upāli:
"You should now know that those of the Śrāvaka vehicle possess distinct skillful means and a distinct profound resolve for upholding the pure precepts; [whereas]..."
Those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle possess distinct skillful means and a distinct profound resolve as they maintain pure precepts.
Why is this? Those who belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle possess distinct skillful means and a distinct profound resolve; [the Bodhisattvas likewise do].
Those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle have distinct skillful means and a distinct profound resolve.
Upāli! Although those of the Śrāvaka vehicle may purely maintain the precepts, they are not said to possess pure precepts from the perspective of the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Although a person of the Bodhisattva vehicle may purely uphold the precepts, they are not said to possess pure precepts from the perspective of the Śrāvaka vehicle. Upāli!
How is it that a person of the Śrāvaka vehicle, though purely upholding the precepts, is not said to possess pure precepts from the perspective of the Bodhisattva vehicle?

Upāli! A person of the Śrāvaka vehicle should not, even for a single thought-moment, give rise to the desire to receive further bodies; this is called the pure observance of precepts by a person of the Śrāvaka vehicle. For a person of the Bodhisattva vehicle, this would be the greatest breach of precepts and is called impure.
What is meant by saying that although a person of the Bodhisattva vehicle maintains pure precepts, they are not called one of pure precepts according to the Śrāvaka vehicle? Upāli!

If a person of the Bodhisattva vehicle is able to endure and accept bodily suffering throughout immeasurable kalpas without giving rise to weariness or aversion, this is called the pure maintenance of precepts for a person of the Bodhisattva vehicle; whereas for a person of the Śrāvaka vehicle, even the greatest violation of precepts would not be called pure.

"Furthermore, Upāli! Those who belong to the Bodhisattva Vehicle uphold the precepts of inexhaustible protection, whereas those who belong to the Śrāvaka Vehicle uphold the precepts of exhaustive protection;
those who belong to the Bodhisattva Vehicle uphold the precepts of open accessibility, whereas those who belong to the Śrāvaka Vehicle uphold the precepts of non-open accessibility."
Those who follow the Bodhisattva vehicle maintain the precepts of profound penetration, while those who follow the Śrāvaka vehicle maintain the precepts of sequential progression. Upāli,

what is meant by those who follow the Bodhisattva vehicle maintaining the precepts of inexhaustible protection, and those who follow the Śrāvaka vehicle maintaining the precepts of exhaustive protection?
When a person of the Bodhisattva vehicle maintains the precepts, they should accord with all sentient beings and others;
a person of the Śrāvaka vehicle should not so accord.

Upāli! For this reason, those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle uphold the precepts of inexhaustible protection, whereas those who belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle uphold the precepts of exhaustive protection. Upāli!
What is meant by those who follow the Bodhisattva vehicle observing the "open" precepts, while those who follow the Śrāvaka vehicle observe the "unopen" precepts? Upāli!

If a person of the Bodhisattva vehicle commits an offense during the first part of the day, yet contemplates at midday that they shall attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), then at that time the Bodhisattva has not violated the integrity of their precept-body.

If a bodhisattva commits a transgression against the precepts during the middle part of the day, but contemplates at the latter part of the day that they shall attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), at that time the bodhisattva does not break the aggregate of morality (*śīlaskandha*).

If he commits a transgression against the precepts during the latter part of the day, he contemplates at the first part of the night that he shall attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*); at that time, the bodhisattva does not break his aggregate of morality (*śīlaskandha*).

If one has committed a transgression against the precepts during the first watch of the night, by contemplating that one shall attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) during the middle watch of the night, the bodhisattva at that time does not break the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*).

If one has committed a transgression against the precepts during the middle watch of the night, but contemplates at the final watch of the night that one shall attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), the bodhisattva at that time does not break the aggregate of morality (*śīlaskandha*).

If one has committed a transgression against the precepts during the latter part of the night, by reflecting at the beginning of the day that one shall attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), the bodhisattva at that time does not break the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*).

For this reason, those who follow the Bodhisattva vehicle uphold the unconditioned precepts (*asaṃvṛta-śīla*), whereas those who follow the Śrāvaka vehicle uphold the conditioned precepts (*saṃvṛta-śīla*); therefore, a bodhisattva should not give rise to great shame (*hrī*), nor should they give rise to the entanglement of great remorse (*kaukṛtya-paryavasthāna*).
Upāli! Those who belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle repeatedly commit offenses and immediately destroy and lose their śrāvaka precept-body. Why is this so?
"Upāli, those who follow the Śrāvaka-yāna should maintain the precepts and sever all fetters as if their heads were on fire, for the sake of their profound resolve toward nirvāṇa."
For this reason, those of the Śrāvaka vehicle are said to uphold the unexpansive precepts.
Upāli! How is it that those of the Bodhisattva vehicle uphold the deeply penetrating precepts, while those of the Śrāvaka vehicle uphold the sequential precepts?

If a person of the Bodhisattva vehicle, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, enjoys the pleasures of the five desires with sovereign ease and experiences all such delights, yet never abandons the resolve for bodhicitta, that Bodhisattva at that time is not said to have lost his precepts.

Why is this? Because those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle, at a later time, will be well able to protect and maintain the bodhicitta; even in their dreams, no afflictions whatsoever shall cause them distress.

A person of the Bodhisattva vehicle should not exhaust all fetters within a single body at once; rather, they should gradually exhaust all fetters, so that their roots of goodness are brought to fulfillment and not left immature.
A person of the Śrāvaka vehicle is like one whose head is on fire; they should not give rise to joy even for a single thought-moment while receiving a body.
For this reason, those of the Mahāyāna uphold the precepts of profound penetration, while those of the Śrāvakayāna uphold the precepts of sequential progression.

Those of the Bodhisattvayāna uphold the precepts of open accessibility and the precepts of inexhaustible protection; those of the Śrāvakayāna uphold the precepts of non-open accessibility and the precepts of exhaustive protection.
Why is this? Because *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is extremely difficult to attain; it can only be accomplished by being fully endowed with great adornments.
A person of the Mahāyāna should not give rise to a mind of weary detachment throughout their coming and going within birth and death over immeasurable eons.

“Upāli! When the Tathāgata observes and deliberates, for the sake of those of the Mahāyāna, he should not exclusively teach the dharma of revulsion, nor should he exclusively teach the dharma of detachment from desire, nor should he exclusively teach the dharma of rapidity.”

One should always speak for them of those dharmas associated with the arousal of a joyful mind; one should always speak for them of the profound, unmixed, and unentangled dharmas free from remorse; and one should always speak for them of the dharmas that are non-accumulative, unobstructed, empty, and non-existent.
"Having heard this Dharma, they will always delight in birth and death without giving rise to sorrow or regret, and they will also be able to fulfill the practices for awakening.
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

There may be those who violate the precepts with a mind associated with desire, or those who violate the precepts with a mind associated with hatred, or those who violate the precepts with a mind associated with delusion.
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva violates the precepts, among those states of mind associated with desire, associated with hatred, and associated with delusion, which is the most serious?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Upāli:

"If there is a bodhisattva who, with a mind associated with desire as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, violates the precepts; or another bodhisattva who, due to a single thought of anger, violates the precepts—both abiding equally in the path of the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna—one should know that the violation committed due to anger is the most grave."
Why is this so? Because of hatred, one is able to abandon sentient beings; because of desire, one gives rise to affection for sentient beings. Upāli!
Regarding all fetters that give rise to affection, a bodhisattva should not feel fear; regarding all fetters that lead to abandoning sentient beings, a bodhisattva should feel great fear.
“Upāli! The Tathāgata previously taught that desire is difficult to abandon and constitutes a minor offense, whereas anger is easy to abandon and is termed a major offense. Upāli!”

All fetters that are minor offenses and easy to abandon should be endured by those of the Mahāyāna; however, all fetters that are major offenses and easy to abandon should not be endured by those of the Mahāyāna, even in their dreams.

For this reason, regarding those in the Mahāyāna who commit an offense out of desire, I say that such a person is not considered to have committed an offense; however, regarding those who commit an offense out of anger, I say that such a person is said to have committed a "great offense," termed a "great affliction" and a "great downfall," which constitutes a major obstacle within the Buddha-dharma.

Upāli! If there is a bodhisattva who lacks skillful means, he feels fear when he violates the precepts with a mind associated with desire, yet he feels no fear when violating the precepts out of anger.

If there is a bodhisattva who possesses skillful means, he may violate the precepts with a mind associated with aversion while feeling fear, yet he does not feel fear when violating the precepts with a mind associated with desire.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, standing amidst the great assembly, stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas are ultimately *vinaya*; who receives this *vinaya*?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If all ordinary beings were already able to fully understand that all phenomena are ultimately *vinaya*, the Tathāgata would never have expounded the *vinaya*."
Because they do not know this, the Tathāgata, in order to cause them to realize the ultimate *parinirvāṇa* of all phenomena, gradually teaches them the various methods of *parinirvāṇa*.
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This Mañjuśrī has explained the definitive meaning of the Vinaya here, yet he has said nothing at all."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī:
"You should now explain the Dharma of the ultimate Vinaya, for this Upāli wishes to hear the meaning of the Vinaya."
At that time, Mañjuśrī said to Upāli: "All dharmas are ultimately stainless;
only by being able to discipline one's own mind can one attain the vision of ultimate vinaya."
When all phenomena are free from the fetters and their intrinsic nature is purified, one is then able to see ultimate *vinaya*.
When all phenomena are free from defilement and a self cannot be apprehended, one is then able to see the *vinaya* of non-regret.
By joyfully practicing and studying hundreds of millions of Dharma-gates according to suchness and reality, one is able to perceive the pure training in the precepts.
Since all dharmas are without discrimination, neither bound nor liberated, and are not objects of discursive thought, one is able to perceive that which is free from bondage and attachment.
All dharmas are without abiding and without defilement; by not remaining or lingering, one is able to see the purity of all dharmas.
All dharmas abide at the limit of space, detached from all locations; by this, one is able to see the purity of what is performed.
All phenomena attain the state of being without conflict, for neither a prior limit nor a subsequent limit can be apprehended; thus one is able to perceive the equality of the three periods of time.
All phenomena are free from all conceptual designations and the mind has no place of activity; thus one is able to perceive the severing of the fetters of doubt.
Upāli! This is called the ultimate Vinaya-dharmadhātu, from which all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have attained the Way.
If one can deliberate upon and observe this Dharma, it is called being well-trained and having attained the most supreme precepts.
"If one does not contemplate this Dharma, then it cannot be called 'deeply entering the precepts studied by the Tathāgata.
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This Dharma taught by Mañjuśrī is entirely inconceivable.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Upāli:
"The Dharma taught by Mañjuśrī relies upon liberation; the liberation upon which it relies is a mind that has neither coming nor going."

Therefore, Mañjuśrī said that all phenomena have no coming or going within the mind; this was spoken in order to eliminate the overweening pride of those who give rise to such pride regarding liberation from the mind.
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By practicing what dharma is a bhikṣu said to be one of overweening pride?”
The Buddha told Upāli:

“If there is a bhikṣu who thinks, ‘I wish to sever greed,’ this is called overweening pride; if he thinks, ‘I wish to sever anger,’ this is called overweening pride; if he thinks, ‘I wish to sever delusion,’ this is called overweening pride.”
To think that the phenomena of desire are distinct from the phenomena of the Buddhas is called overweening pride.
To think that the phenomena of hatred are distinct from the phenomena of the Buddhas is called overweening pride.
To conceive that the dharmas of ignorance are distinct and the dharmas of the Buddhas are distinct is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

To conceive and perceive that there is something attained is called overweening pride; to conceive and perceive that there is something realized is called overweening pride; to conceive and perceive that there is liberation is called overweening pride; to conceive and perceive that all dharmas are empty is called overweening pride; to conceive and perceive the signless (*animitta*) is called overweening pride; to conceive and perceive the wishless (*apraṇihita*) is called overweening pride; to conceive and perceive that there are conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) is called overweening pride; to conceive and perceive that there are dharmas is called overweening pride.
"All dharmas are inconceivable"—to entertain such a thought and yet consider it inappropriate to contemplate them is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
"All dharmas are empty and non-existent; what is the use of diligence?"—to entertain such a thought is called overweening pride.
This is called the śrāvaka abiding in overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
What is called the bodhisattva’s overweening pride?
To think, "The Buddha-vehicle is supreme," and then to resolve, "I shall generate the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) therein," is called overweening pride.
To think, "By practicing the six pāramitās, one shall attain Buddhahood," is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
To think, "The prajñāpāramitā alone can bring about liberation, and there is no other dharma by which one may attain liberation," is called overweening pride.
To apply skillful means toward the profound Dharma while not relying on worldly dharmas, yet to harbor such thoughts, is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
To think, "This dharma is profound" or "This is not profound," and to harbor such thoughts, is called overweening pride.
To think, "This dharma is pure; this dharma is not pure," is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
To think, "This is the Buddha-dharma; this is the Pratyekabuddha-dharma; this is the Śrāvaka-dharma," is called overweening pride.
To think, "This dharma should be practiced; this dharma should not be practiced," is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
To think, "This is a proximate dharma; this is not a proximate dharma," is called overweening pride.
To think, "This is the right path; this is the wrong path," is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
To think, "I shall quickly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; I shall not quickly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," is called overweening pride.
"All Buddha-dharmas are inconceivable; no one has ever been able to awaken to them. To engage in such reflection is called *adhimāna* (conceit).
"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is inconceivable; it should not be conceptualized. This is not a true vision but rather a fault; this is what is called a bodhisattva abiding in conceit.
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How does a bhikṣu become free from overweening pride?"
The Buddha told Upāli:
“If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates all states of mind, and while contemplating the mind does not become attached to that contemplation, this is called the supreme freedom from overweening pride.”
At that time, wishing to analyze and contemplate the Dharma in detail, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One should not discriminate between what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma; One should not dwell in the conceptual proliferation of various minds.
One who is able to know the inconceivable Dharma Is called a person who experiences happiness at all times."
If there are those who wish to know whether things exist or do not exist, such contemplation is not true;
they are ordinary persons following after a deviant mind, undergoing hundreds of thousands of billions of sufferings within the realms of existence.
If there is a bhikṣu who constantly recollects the Buddha, this is neither true nor right mindfulness;
one should know that the Buddha arises from conceptual discrimination, and in reality, he is neither graspable nor produced.
If one contemplates all phenomena as empty, such a person dwells on a deviant path and is but an ordinary worldling;
though they speak of the dharma of emptiness by means of names and designations, in reality there are no names or designations by which it can be spoken.
Dwelling in seclusion and tranquility, one contemplates the Dharma; such a person is praised by the world as one who abides in stillness.

Yet, for the mind to dwell in applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) is mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); therefore, it is through the absence of such thinking that one can truly understand the Dharma.
The various phenomena of mind and mind-objects are called volition; if there is volition, there will necessarily be attachment.
If one can distance oneself from these dharmas of attachment, one will no longer have volitions regarding those objects of thought.
Dharmas are identical to grass and trees, possessing no cognition; yet they arise through various conditions.
No sentient being can be found who is able to give rise to these empty and non-existent dharmas of conditions.
It is by means of the light of the sun that the eye is able to see; at night it does not see, being devoid of such conditions.
If the eye were inherently capable of seeing forms, why would it not see when lacking those conditions?
The eye constantly relies upon various lights to perceive diverse and pleasing forms;
one should know that the nature of seeing arises from manifold conditions, and therefore the eye itself cannot see.
If one hears any pleasant sounds, they arise and immediately perish, leaving nothing to be heard;
their place of departure cannot be found, for it is only through conceptual discrimination that the perception of sound arises.
All phenomena share the same sound; they are provisionally designated with various numerical characteristics.
Yet these have never been able to give rise to either dharma or non-dharma; they are manifested only for the sake of ordinary beings.
I praise the giving of alms for the sake of the world, yet in truth, the stinginess regarding the Dharma cannot be found;
the Dharma taught by the Buddha is inconceivable, and though it cannot be grasped, it is proclaimed.

I constantly praise and speak of upholding the pure precepts; the characteristics of breaking the precepts are like grasping at emptiness, and all forms of violating the precepts are like space—pure observance of the precepts is likewise so.
I declare that patience is supreme; the nature of anger does not truly arise.
Since there is no provocation among all phenomena, the Buddha has revealed the practice of patience.
He constantly speaks day and night without weariness; awakening and diligence are supreme.
Though he may practice diligently for a hundred eons, what he accomplishes neither increases nor decreases.
Meditative concentration and liberation are supreme; the Tathāgata has revealed and taught these various gateways.
Yet in reality, all phenomena are without distraction; the World-Honored One now speaks of these meditative concentrations.
The nature of wisdom is that which can awaken to and understand; one who knows all phenomena is a person of wisdom.
Yet their intrinsic nature is without arising, which the Buddha can manifest and explain.
I constantly praise and speak of the dharma of purity and austerity;
those who joyfully delight in practicing the dhūtas seek out the nature of greed but find it unobtainable, and are thus called the supreme non-greedy ones.
Constantly for the sake of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, you manifest and preach the terrors of the hells;
yet never has there been one who, having gone, fell into the evil realms, or died and entered the Avīci Hell.
There is no one who creates hell, nor is there anyone who creates spears, lances, and the like;
it is through conceptual discrimination that they appear to exist, and thus the harm of swords and blades wounds one's own body.
Trees adorned with various colors, flowers, and fruits, and golden palaces shining brilliantly—none of these ever had a creator;
they all arise from the conceptualization of false imagination.
The deceptive dharma deludes the world; ordinary persons revolve within it through clinging to conceptions.
Since grasping and non-grasping lack intrinsic nature, they are like the discrimination of illusions and mirages.
Those who speak of the most excellent among all conditioned phenomena can inspire the aspiration for the Way in sentient beings;
yet since the path to Bodhi cannot be apprehended, one should know that the seeker, too, is not real.
The intrinsic nature of that mind is eternally pure, Free from all defilements and afflictions;
Yet ordinary beings discriminate with various evil minds, Spontaneously giving rise to craving and all manner of attachments.
All phenomena are wondrous, supreme, and eternally tranquil; in reality, they possess no craving, hatred, or delusion.
The nature of phenomena is liberation, free from defiled attachment, reaching the state of peace that has no fixed location.
I know all phenomena to be like space; Wandering through all worlds, I give rise to no fear.
My mind has never been subject to defilement or attachment; Therefore, I do not abide in the paths of error.
Throughout many kalpas I have cultivated various practices to deliver and liberate boundless sentient beings;
yet these beings are never exhausted, nor has there ever been a time when their number increased or decreased.
For example, suppose there were a great master of illusion in the world, Who could conjure forth boundless hundreds of thousands of beings;
If he were to instantly slay all those conjured persons, There would be no increase or decrease to the master of illusion himself.
All sentient beings are like illusory forms; Their limits can never be found.
If there are those who can contemplate this inconceivability, One should know that such persons do not weary of birth.
Contemplating the tranquility of the world is called valor; knowing the true nature of phenomena is likewise so.
One should practice while experiencing the benefits of the five desires, yet without giving rise to attachment, thereby delivering sentient beings.
There are no sentient beings and no life-span; yet the World-Honored One, out of compassion, gives rise to loving-kindness and pity.
He diligently practices great asceticism with vigor, even though there are no sentient beings for whom he performs benefit.
It is like using an empty fist to entice a small child, deceiving his mind and causing him to become attached;
then, when the hand is opened to reveal the empty fist, the child immediately bursts into loud weeping.

Thus is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, inconceivable; with a pure awakened mind regarding the characteristics of all phenomena, having already realized the state of emptiness and the absence of dharmas, he is nevertheless able to manifest within the world.
Within my Dharma there is great joy; having cast off worldly garments and been able to go forth, one shall later attain the most supreme fruit—so it is spoken by the One of Great Compassion.
Having already been able to leave the household life and abandon worldly affairs, you further hear that you shall attain the various fruits;
yet upon observing the true nature of all phenomena, there are no fruits whatsoever that can be attained.
Having attained no fruit among all dharmas, you have further given rise to that which was never before;
how wonderful is the Greatly Compassionate Lion among Men, who skillfully enters into the corresponding characteristics of all dharmas!

All phenomena are like space; though one may establish hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of names for them—such as the foundations, dhyānas, and liberations—they are also called the powers and the factors of enlightenment.
The sense faculties have no characteristic of arising or ceasing; the powers of awakening and other such dharmas are likewise so.
They are not of the nature of form and cannot be grasped; yet by the power of wisdom, they are manifested to the world.
I say that when sentient beings have something attained, it is all merely a departure from the characteristics of intrinsic nature;
if one calculates that there is a self which has something attained, this is not called attaining the fruits of the śramaṇa.
If dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, who could therein obtain anything?
To say that sentient beings obtain is to say there is no obtaining; one who can awaken to this dharma is said to have obtained it.
Sentient beings who attain the fruit are called "most excellent," yet I say that sentient beings are not [truly] sentient beings;
since there has never been anyone who attains a sentient being, therefore there should be no attainment of the fruit.
Just as a fertile field will not produce sprouts if there are no seeds,
so too, since sentient beings cannot be found, how could there ever be the attainment of tranquility?
The nature of all sentient beings is quiescent; Never has anyone found its root.
If there be one who can contemplate this Dharma, I say they shall attain eternal stillness, with nothing remaining.
The hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas of the past have delivered all sentient beings without end;
yet these sentient beings lack any true reality, for they are ultimately quiescent and never again born.
All phenomena possess the characteristic of cessation; none have ever been able to arise.
If one can contemplate all phenomena in this way, that person will not be attached to the triple world.
I declare that all paths are without obstruction; Able to leave behind all attachments, they are most delightful.

Extremely difficult to encounter in hundreds of thousands of kalpas, It was from the past Buddha Dīpaṃkara That one was able to give rise to the supreme patience regarding non-arising, Permanently severing all obstructions without remainder.
Having attained pure mindfulness as their life-force, they are forever free from all false views.
They have no evil realms and dwell in constant peace and joy; with valor, they are able to know the unobstructed Dharma.
Unattached to all conditioned formations, they attain liberation; throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they give rise to no fear.
It is not difficult to attain the various eloquences, nor the boundless hundreds of thousands of dhāraṇīs;
by understanding the meanings and purports of these dhāraṇīs, one can swiftly awaken to the unimpeded Dharma.
When these verses had been spoken, two hundred bhikṣus who were conceited attained liberation of mind by not grasping at any dharmas;
six thousand bodhisattvas (the text notes "sixty" in an alternate version) attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named, and how should it be upheld?”
The Buddha told Upāli:
"This sutra is named 'Definitive Vinaya,' and it is also named 'Destroying All Consciousness'; you should uphold it."

At that time, Upāli, Mañjuśrī, and the entire great assembly—including devas, humans, asuras, and others—having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sūtra on the Definitive Vinaya Spoken by the Buddha.
